summary:
Seychelles decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2016 with the repeal of Penal Code Section 151, a colonial-era provision that had carried up to 14 years' imprisonment for male same-sex intimacy.

The Constitution of Seychelles guarantees freedom from torture under Article 16 and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex under Article 27. The source text listing those grounds does not name gender identity expressly.

Section 5 of the Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) adds sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status to the protected characteristics, creating an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences.

The revised law increases prison sentences for violent crimes motivated by hostility toward a victim's sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability. The Human Dignity Trust describes Seychelles, after South Africa, as the second African country to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation.

Seychelles does not recognise same-sex marriage or same-sex civil unions. In June 2015 two men, one British and one Seychellois national, were married at the British High Commission in Seychelles by High Commissioner Lindsay Skoll, a ceremony performed under foreign mission authority rather than Seychellois law.

Legal and social conditions for visitors continue to vary from the statutory position; the statutory framework is protective, but the sources do not document enforcement practice or day-to-day experience for trans travellers.
tangentialFactors:
The 2016 repeal was reported internationally as a significant legal change for the islands, with coverage framing Seychelles as a holiday destination opening itself to LGBT people. Press framing of this kind does not establish the level of social acceptance a trans visitor will encounter.

Seychelles' 2024 hate-crime provisions place it alongside South Africa in the African regional context as a jurisdiction with broad hate-based victimisation protections, a comparative position that distinguishes it from most neighbouring legal systems.
localsOnly:
Residents benefit from the Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024), which raises sentences for violent offences motivated by hostility toward the listed protected characteristics, including gender identity and sex characteristics.

The Constitution's Article 27 non-discrimination guarantee covers sex; gender identity is not named in the enumerated grounds as reported by the source.

Same-sex couples have no access to marriage or civil union recognition under Seychellois law; the June 2015 British High Commission ceremony did not create recognition under domestic statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2024 enhanced-protection provisions have been applied in any reported prosecution is unresolved in the sources; no enforcement case is documented.

The sources do not address legal gender recognition, marker changes on identity documents, or any screening process that could expose a trans traveller's gender history at entry; these remain not sourced.

Facilities access, healthcare restrictions, and any documented incidents of violence against trans visitors in Seychelles are not covered by the inventory and remain unresolved.
